title: We've flown a radiation-blocking vest to the Moon and back, and it worked
gist: StemRad's AstroRad vest, flown on Artemis I aboard the phantom torso Zohar, was modeled to cut effective radiation dose by roughly 60 percent in a 1972-style solar storm and 40 percent in a harder 1989-type event — comparable to Orion's dedicated storm shelter but without immobilizing the crew, though it does nothing against galactic cosmic rays and the results rest on simulation rather than a real storm.

themes.theme: Selective shielding as a mass-efficiency framework

insights.claim: StemRad's core thesis is to shield the astronaut rather than the spacecraft, because mass is the binding constraint in space radiation protection and no spacecraft built so far carries enough shielding to stop solar proton events.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Mass-per-unit-protection is the metric that decides which radiation solutions get flown — applies equally to habitat design and deep-space mission architecture.
insights.quote: The question was how to use mass in a very efficient way. Mass is really the bottleneck—every gram counts.

insights.claim: The human body is not uniformly radiation-vulnerable — bone marrow is far more sensitive than the brain — so protecting even a fraction of bone marrow allows a person to regrow it and survive high-dose exposure, which is the biological basis for partial-body shielding.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Organ-weighted risk modeling unlocks order-of-magnitude mass savings that whole-body shielding cannot achieve — the key insight commercializable beyond spaceflight.
insights.quote: Tissues like the bone marrow are a lot more sensitive to radiation compared to the brain
insights.locator: StemRad engineers, though, figured dressing as a medieval knight

insights.claim: AstroRad reduces effective radiation dose by 60 percent without protecting the head, arms or legs at all — covering only hips, breasts, stomach, colon and reproductive organs.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A counterintuitive result that overturns the full-armor assumption and makes wearable shielding viable at reasonable mass.
insights.quote: we're actually able to reduce the effective dose by 60 percent without protecting the head, the arms, or even the legs

insights.claim: StemRad's approach originated in a terrestrial product — a belt for nuclear first responders worn around the hips, which hold roughly half the body's bone marrow — later expanded with Lockheed Martin into the female-form space vest.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Dual-use terrestrial and space markets give the shielding technology a revenue base independent of slow-moving NASA program timelines.
insights.locator: Following this idea, StemRad developed a belt

insights.claim: Shielding effectiveness is governed primarily by a material's atomic number divided by atomic mass, which is why hydrogen — with roughly double the ratio of any other element — makes water and high-density polyethylene superior shields to lead.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A first-principles selection rule that inverts intuition about dense materials — the design constraint for any deep-space habitat or shielding supplier.
insights.quote: The primary factor in how effective a shielding material is is its atomic number divided by its atomic mass

insights.claim: StemRad solved HDPE's stiffness problem by dividing the shielding panels into thousands of hexagonal tessellated rods of varying length and cross-section sandwiched between elastic fabric layers, producing a vest that behaves almost like water while remaining solid.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: The tessellation approach is the actual defensible IP — the material is commodity plastic; the geometry is what makes it wearable.
insights.quote: We divided up the shielding panels into thousands of hexagonal tessellated rods of HDPE
insights.locator: The problem with a solid, rather stiff material like HDPE

insights.claim: Rod lengths in the vest run 9 to 60 millimeters, calculated using the Bethe-Bloch formula describing how charged particles lose energy through matter, so the team could predict stopping distance for a given particle energy.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Physics-derived rather than empirically tuned geometry means the design scales predictably to other radiation environments and body sites.
insights.locator: The rods run 9 to 60 millimeters long

themes.theme: Artemis I test methodology and its limits

insights.claim: Artemis I carried two identical tissue-equivalent phantom torsos, Helga and Zohar, adapted from radiotherapy dosimetry phantoms and packed with thousands of dosimeters tracking dose by flight phase — with only Zohar wearing the AstroRad vest.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A paired-control design on an uncrewed flight is the cheapest way to generate flight-qualified human-factors data — a template for other crew-safety hardware.

insights.claim: No solar storm occurred during Artemis I, so the team used the mission's Van Allen inner-belt crossing as a proxy since belt proton energies roughly overlap those in a typical storm, then validated Monte Carlo models against the dosimeters to within five percent per dosimeter.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Five percent model-to-measurement agreement is what converts a single flight opportunity into a general-purpose simulation capability.
insights.quote: The output of the models was, for each dosimeter, within five percent of the actual measured data.
insights.locator: Most of the radiation all these detectors recorded

insights.claim: The vest's protection claim rests mainly on computer models carrying known uncertainties — a simplified two-material stand-in for Orion's hull and a statistically predicted rather than directly recorded Van Allen belt spectrum.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: The headline efficacy numbers are simulation outputs, not flight measurements of the actual threat — discount accordingly when assessing readiness.
insights.quote: the protection we think it offers as it is today rests mainly on computer models
insights.locator: The problem is, the AstroRad vest is unlikely

insights.claim: Obtaining real rather than simulated performance data would require flying the vest on an Orion spacecraft into deep space and waiting for a solar storm to occur, which the author calls hardly feasible.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: The validation gap is structural and will not close before crews need the hardware — a permanent residual risk in deep-space mission planning.
insights.locator: Getting real, not simulated, data on the vest's performance

themes.theme: Performance envelope and what it does not cover

insights.claim: Simulations swapping in historical solar storm spectra showed the vest cut effective dose by around 60 percent for a 1972-style event but only about 40 percent for the harder, higher-energy 1989-type storm.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Protection degrades exactly when the threat is worst — the worst-case-storm number, not the typical one, should drive mission risk models.
insights.quote: The vest cut the effective radiation dose by around 60 percent for the 1972-style event but only about 40 percent for the 1989-like storm.

insights.claim: The performance gap exists because solar storm particle flux is normally dominated by lower-energy protons with high-energy ones exponentially rarer, so shielding works well against the bulk of typical events but poorly against hard-spectrum outliers.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Spectrum hardness, not total flux, is the variable that determines shielding adequacy — the parameter to specify in any radiation-protection requirement.
insights.quote: The bulk of that radiation is in the lower energy range, where you can shield it with a reasonable amount of material

insights.claim: Wearing the vest during a single major storm would extend an astronaut's career by roughly 40 to 193 days measured against NASA's 600-millisievert lifetime dose limit.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Career-days-per-storm is the operational metric that translates radiation shielding into crew-utilization economics for long-duration programs.

insights.claim: The vest delivers protection comparable to Orion's dedicated storm shelter but without confining the crew, since astronauts in the shelter cannot move or perform mission operations — StemRad positions it as complementary rather than a replacement.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Preserving crew productivity during a multi-day storm is the actual value proposition — mission-hours saved, not just dose reduced.
insights.quote: With the vest, they'd be able to enjoy the same amount of protection while continuing to move around the cabin. We see it as a protection complementary to the storm shelter
insights.locator: That's comparable to Orion's dedicated storm shelter

insights.claim: The vest does nearly nothing against galactic cosmic rays, which arrive continuously at much higher energies and would require wearing it at all times — leaving the dominant chronic deep-space radiation risk unaddressed.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: GCR remains the unsolved problem gating Mars-duration missions; no wearable approach closes it, so habitat or active shielding solutions retain their market.
insights.quote: Using the vest against these rays would not be reasonable. You'd have to wear it at all times.
insights.locator: The vest, though, does nearly nothing

themes.theme: Roadmap: cut mass, not add protection

insights.claim: The AstroRad vest as flown on Artemis I weighed 26 kilograms — roughly a full suit of medieval plate armor — and StemRad says improving protection further would be hard without adding mass.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: The design has hit a physical protection-per-mass ceiling, which is why the roadmap pivots to weight reduction rather than efficacy gains.
insights.locator: But an even bigger constraint for this design

insights.claim: Using Artemis I data StemRad has already cut vest weight from 26 kilograms to 16 without losing a large part of the protection, targeting a garment light enough for astronauts to wear for days around a storm's peak rather than only during it.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A 38 percent mass cut with minimal efficacy loss changes wear-duration economics — the metric that determines whether crews actually use it.
insights.quote: That reduction came without losing a large part of the protection
